/ai/foundations/what-is-an-llm.def: A large language model (LLM) is a program trained on a huge amount of text to predict the next token (a small piece of a word). By predicting one token after another, it writes answers, summaries and code.
/ai/foundations/what-is-an-llm.why: Writing rules by hand for every language task is impossible. Training one model on a huge amount of text gives a single tool that can handle many tasks from plain instructions. The price is that it produces likely text, not checked facts.
use: You need to understand, write, summarise, translate or classify text
You can describe the task in plain language or with a few examples
A mistake can be caught by a person or a check
avoid: You need exact, always-correct answers (calculations, lookups in a database)
The answer depends on information the model cannot see
A wrong answer would be costly and nothing checks it

/ai/foundations/tokens-and-context-windo.def: A token is the small piece of text a model reads and writes, roughly four characters of English. The context window is the maximum number of tokens the model can handle in one call, counting your input and its answer together.
/ai/foundations/tokens-and-context-windo.why: Models cannot work on raw letters or unlimited text. Splitting text into tokens gives a fixed vocabulary to work with, and the window limits how much one call can hold. Tokens are also what providers charge for.
use: You check whether a prompt fits before you send it
You estimate cost, speed or rate limits
You decide how much history and how many documents to include
avoid: You count characters or words and assume that is the limit
You fill the whole window because it is allowed
You reuse token counts from one model for another

/ai/foundations/credits-pricing-cost.def: LLM providers charge per token, with separate prices for input and output tokens. Credits are a prepaid balance that is spent as you use the service.
/ai/foundations/credits-pricing-cost.why: Running large models costs real compute for every token. Per-token pricing makes the bill follow usage, and prepaid credits let you cap what you can spend. Without tracking, one long prompt or one looping agent can use up the balance.
use: You plan the monthly cost of an AI feature before building it
You choose between a small and a large model
You set budgets and alerts per user or feature
avoid: You judge cost by the price per token alone, without counting tokens per call
You send the full history on every call without trimming
You hard-code prices that providers change often

/ai/prompting/prompt-engineering.def: Prompt engineering is writing the input to a model so that it gives useful, reliable output. A good prompt states the task, gives the needed context and examples, and says what format to answer in.
/ai/prompting/prompt-engineering.why: A model does exactly what the text tells it, so unclear instructions give unclear answers. Better prompts improve results without retraining the model, which makes them the cheapest first thing to try.
use: The model gives the right kind of answer but not reliably
You need a fixed output format that your code can read
You want to improve quality without changing the model
avoid: The model lacks the information, since wording cannot add facts (use retrieval)
You judge a prompt from one or two answers
The prompt keeps growing with patches after every bug

/ai/prompting/context-engineering.def: Context engineering is choosing what information the model sees on each call: instructions, tools, documents, history and memory. The aim is the smallest set of information that lets the model do the task well.
/ai/prompting/context-engineering.why: Prompts alone are not enough once an application runs many steps. The context fills with history and tool results, which costs money, slows calls and distracts the model. Managing it on purpose keeps answers accurate.
use: The application runs many steps or long conversations (agents, chat)
You add documents or tool results to the model input
Answers get worse or costs grow as sessions get longer
avoid: The task is a single short call, where plain prompt wording is enough
You add everything just in case
You keep every old tool result in the history

/ai/retrieval/embeddings-vector-database.def: An embedding is a list of numbers that represents the meaning of a text, so texts with similar meaning have similar numbers. A vector database stores embeddings and quickly finds the ones closest to a query.
/ai/retrieval/embeddings-vector-database.why: Keyword search misses answers that use different words, such as "money back" versus "refund". Embeddings let you search by meaning, and a vector database makes that fast on large collections.
use: You search by meaning rather than exact words
You build retrieval for RAG
You find similar items (documents, products, questions)
avoid: You need exact matches for ids, codes or names (use keyword search or both)
You have only a few documents that fit in the prompt
You would add a separate vector engine before checking whether pgvector is enough

/ai/retrieval/rag.def: RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) means finding the most relevant pieces of your own data and putting them in the prompt, so the model answers from them. The model uses your documents instead of relying only on what it learned in training.
/ai/retrieval/rag.why: A model does not know your private documents or recent events, and it may invent answers when it lacks facts. RAG supplies the facts at question time without retraining, and lets you show sources.
use: Answers must come from private or frequently changing documents
Users need sources they can check
The knowledge base is too large to put in every prompt
avoid: You want to change the model's style or behaviour (use prompting or fine-tuning)
Only a few short documents are needed (put them straight into the prompt)
You have no way to test whether retrieval finds the right text

/ai/agents/ai-agents.def: An AI agent is a program where an LLM decides the next step in a loop, using tools. The model asks for an action, your code runs it, the result goes back to the model, and this repeats until the task is done or a limit is reached.
/ai/agents/ai-agents.why: Some tasks cannot be written as fixed steps, because what to do next depends on what was just found. An agent lets the model choose the steps, so one system can handle open-ended work. That freedom needs limits to stay safe and affordable.
use: The steps depend on what is found along the way (research, debugging, multi-step lookups)
The task needs several tools combined
A person can review risky actions
avoid: The steps are known in advance (use a fixed workflow: cheaper and more predictable)
A mistake is costly and cannot be approved or undone
You cannot set step, budget and permission limits

/ai/foundations/fine-tuning-and-model-ch.def: Fine-tuning means training an existing model further on your own examples, so its behaviour, style or format changes. Choosing a model means testing candidates on your task and picking the cheapest one that is good enough.
/ai/foundations/fine-tuning-and-model-ch.why: A general model is not always right for your task, and the largest model is slow and costly. Fine-tuning adapts behaviour, and careful model choice and routing keep quality up and cost down.
use: A prompt cannot give you a consistent style, format or narrow skill
A small model must match a large one on one task (distillation)
You choose or switch models and want evidence from your own tests
avoid: You want to teach facts that change (use RAG)
You have not tried a better prompt first
You pick a model from a leaderboard without testing your own cases

/ai/prompting/structured-output-and-tool.def: Structured output makes a model reply in a fixed shape, usually JSON that your code can read. Tool calling lets the model ask your code to run a function, and then continue with the result.
/ai/prompting/structured-output-and-tool.why: A program cannot do much with a paragraph of prose, and a model alone cannot look things up or change anything. These two features let a model fit into normal software: it returns data you can parse and asks for actions you can control.
use: Your code needs a label, number or record from the model
The model needs live data or must trigger an action
You want to validate and limit what the model can do
avoid: A plain text answer is enough
You would pass model-made arguments straight to a database, shell or URL
You give the model many overlapping tools

/ai/agents/model-context-protocol.def: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard for connecting AI applications to tools and data. A server exposes tools, resources and prompts, and any MCP-capable application can use them.
/ai/agents/model-context-protocol.why: Without a standard, every AI application needs a custom connector for every tool, so the work multiplies. With MCP you write a connector once as a server and many applications can use it.
use: You want one tool or data source available to several AI applications
You use ready-made servers for common systems
You want a standard way to describe tools to agents
avoid: One application needs one simple function (a normal tool is enough)
You would install a server you cannot trust or review
You connect many servers and flood the context with tool descriptions

/ai/agents/multi-agent-patterns.def: A multi-agent system uses several model-driven agents that work together, each with its own instructions, tools and context. Common patterns are orchestrator and workers, pipelines, parallel work, routers and evaluator loops.
/ai/agents/multi-agent-patterns.why: One agent can run out of context, cannot do independent work in parallel, and holds all permissions at once. Splitting the work solves those problems, at the price of more tokens and more to manage.
use: One context cannot hold the work
Sub-tasks are independent and can run in parallel
Different parts need different tools or permissions
avoid: A single agent or a fixed workflow would work
You cannot cap steps and budget for each agent
The hand-offs would be long free text

/ai/safety/guardrails-and-safety.def: Guardrails are checks and limits in your code around a model: on inputs, outputs, actions and resource use. The model suggests, and your code decides what is allowed.
/ai/safety/guardrails-and-safety.why: A model can be wrong, can be tricked and can ignore instructions in a prompt. Code checks are the only reliable way to stop a bad output or action from causing harm.
use: The model can trigger actions or show text to users
Mistakes would be costly or hard to undo
You need an audit trail of what was allowed or blocked
avoid: You rely on the prompt alone to enforce rules
Filters block so much that users work around them
Everything is allowed except a short banned list

/ai/safety/prompt-injection-and-security.def: Prompt injection is when text from an untrusted source contains instructions and the model follows them. It can come from the user (direct) or hide in content the model reads, such as a web page or email (indirect).
/ai/safety/prompt-injection-and-security.why: A model treats instructions and data as the same thing, text, and cannot reliably tell them apart. So untrusted content can steer it, and the system must be designed so that even a fooled model cannot do serious harm.
use: The model reads outside content (web, email, documents, tool results)
The model has tools that send data or change things
You review an AI feature for security
avoid: You trust a firm sentence in the system prompt as protection
One session has private data, untrusted content and outbound actions together
Tools run with system-wide rights instead of the user's

/ai/production/evals-and-testing.def: Evals are repeatable tests that run an LLM feature over many realistic cases and score the results. They show whether a change made things better or worse.
/ai/production/evals-and-testing.why: Model answers vary, and a small change to a prompt, model or document can shift results across many cases. A few manual tries cannot show that, so you measure on a fixed set.
use: Before changing a prompt, model, retrieval or tool
To gate releases in your build pipeline
To compare models and prompt versions on your own cases
avoid: You judge a change from two or three examples
The set has only easy cases
You trust a model judge without checking it against people

/ai/production/observability-latency-cac.def: Observability means recording enough about every model call (tokens, latency, cost, prompt version, tool calls) to explain what happened. Latency work and caching make the feature faster and cheaper.
/ai/production/observability-latency-cac.why: Model calls are slow, costly and variable. Without records you cannot explain a wrong or slow answer, or a surprising bill, and without caching and limits you pay for repeated work and fail under rate limits.
use: Any LLM feature in production
You need to find the cause of slow or wrong answers
You need to control cost and survive provider limits and outages
avoid: You log full prompts with personal data and keep them forever
You use semantic caching with a loose threshold
You cache private answers without the user in the key

/ai/production/spring-ai-and-langchain4j.def: Spring AI and LangChain4j are Java libraries for working with LLMs. They handle messages, structured output, tools, RAG, memory and many providers, so you do not write that plumbing yourself.
/ai/production/spring-ai-and-langchain4j.why: Calling a model API directly means repeating the same code for messages, parsing, the tool loop and vector stores. A library does that once and lets you switch providers more easily.
use: You build Java services that call LLMs (Spring AI for Spring Boot, LangChain4j for any Java)
You need tools, RAG or structured output quickly
You want one interface over several providers
avoid: You spread library types through all business code
You copy examples written for another version
You let the library run tool loops with no limits

/system-design/design-a-rag-chatbot.def: A RAG chatbot answers employee questions from company documents. An ingestion pipeline builds a searchable index, and for each question the system retrieves allowed chunks, builds a prompt and generates an answer with citations.
/system-design/design-a-rag-chatbot.why: Employees cannot find answers across thousands of documents, and a plain model does not know the company's private or changing information. RAG supplies the right text at question time, with sources and permission checks.
use: Answers must come from private or changing documents
Users need citations they can check
Different users may read different documents
avoid: A few short documents fit in the prompt
You cannot enforce permissions at retrieval
Nobody will measure answer quality

/system-design/design-an-ai-agent-platfo.def: An AI agent platform runs agents for many teams. It queues runs, executes the agent loop with saved state, routes model calls through a gateway, runs tools in sandboxes, asks humans for approval and tracks cost and traces.
/system-design/design-an-ai-agent-platfo.why: Every team building agents alone would repeat the same hard parts: crash recovery, safety, limits, credentials and cost control. A shared platform solves them once and keeps teams isolated.
use: Several teams run agents and need shared limits, safety and accounting
Runs are long, call many tools and sometimes wait for approval
You need audit, cost control and isolation
avoid: One team has one simple agent (a library is enough)
You would build a platform before you know what agents you need
You cannot staff it or buy it managed

/java/core-java/oop-and-design/encapsula.def: Encapsulation means keeping an object's data private and letting other code change it only through methods. The object can then protect its own rules, so it never ends up in an invalid state.

example.title: A bank account that protects its balance

/java/core-java/oop-and-design/abstracti.def: Abstraction means showing what something does and hiding how it does it. In Java you describe the "what" with an interface or an abstract class, and callers depend on that instead of on a concrete class.

example.title: Checkout does not care how the payment is made

/java/core-java/oop-and-design/inheritan.def: Inheritance lets a class reuse and extend another class with `extends`. The child class gets the parent's fields and methods and can add new ones or change existing ones. Use it for a true "is-a" relationship.

example.title: A manager is an employee with extras

/java/core-java/oop-and-design/polymorph.def: Polymorphism means one call can run different code depending on the real object. You call a method on a parent type, and Java picks the child's version while the program runs.

example.title: One loop, three different areas

/java/core-java/oop-and-design/compositi.def: Composition means building a class by holding other objects and using them, instead of extending a class. It keeps classes loosely coupled and easy to change, so it is usually preferred over inheritance when you only want to reuse behaviour.

example.title: A notifier that can swap how it sends messages

/java/core-java/oop-and-design/interface.def: An interface describes what a type can do and holds no state. An abstract class can also hold shared fields and partly finished code. A class can implement many interfaces but extend only one class.

example.title: An abstract base class plus an interface

/java/core-java/oop-and-design/single-re.def: The single responsibility principle says a class should have one reason to change. Each class does one job, so a change to one concern does not break another.

example.title: Calculating an invoice and printing it are two jobs

/java/core-java/oop-and-design/open-clos.def: The open/closed principle says code should be open for extension but closed for modification. You add new behaviour by adding new classes, not by editing code that already works.

example.title: Adding a new discount without touching the checkout

/java/core-java/oop-and-design/liskov-su.def: The Liskov substitution principle says a child class must work anywhere its parent is expected, without surprising the caller. If code that works with the parent breaks when it gets the child, the hierarchy is wrong.

example.title: A Square that breaks code written for Rectangle, and a fix

/java/core-java/oop-and-design/interface.def: The interface segregation principle says no class should be forced to implement methods it does not use. Prefer several small interfaces over one big one.

example.title: A basic printer is not forced to scan

/java/core-java/oop-and-design/dependenc.def: The dependency inversion principle says high-level code should depend on an abstraction, not on a concrete class. The concrete class is passed in from outside, which makes it easy to swap and to test.

example.title: A service that gets its sender from outside

/java/core-java/generics/generic-classes.def: A generic class works with a type that you choose when you use it, written like `Box<String>`. The compiler checks the type for you, so you do not need casts.

example.title: A box that holds any one type, and a pair of two types

/java/core-java/generics/generic-methods.def: A generic method has its own type parameter, written before the return type. Java works out the type from the arguments, so one method can serve many types safely.

example.title: One method that works for any list or array

/java/core-java/generics/bounded-types.def: A bounded type parameter limits which types are allowed, using `extends`. Inside the method you can then call the methods of the bound, such as `compareTo`.

example.title: A max method that only accepts things that can be compared

/java/core-java/generics/wildcards.def: A wildcard `?` stands for "some unknown type". `? extends Number` means "Number or any subtype", which is good for reading. `?` alone means any type at all.

example.title: Summing a list of any number type

/java/core-java/generics/pecs.def: PECS means: if a collection only gives you values, use `? extends T` (producer extends). If it only receives values, use `? super T` (consumer super). It makes a method accept more types while staying type-safe.

example.title: Copy from a producer into a consumer

/java/core-java/generics/type-erasure.def: Type erasure means generic type arguments exist only at compile time. At run time `List<String>` and `List<Integer>` are both just `List`, so you cannot ask a list what type it holds.

example.title: Two different lists, the same class at run time

/java/core-java/exceptions/checked-vs-un.def: A checked exception must be caught or declared with `throws`, so the compiler makes you deal with it. An unchecked exception (a `RuntimeException`) needs no declaration and usually means a bug in the code.

example.title: Reading a missing file (checked) and bad input (unchecked)

/java/core-java/exceptions/try-catch-fin.def: Code that might fail goes in `try`. `catch` handles a specific problem, and `finally` always runs afterwards, whether or not an exception happened. Catch the most specific exception first.

example.title: Parsing a number, with cleanup that always runs

/java/core-java/exceptions/try-with-reso.def: try-with-resources closes things like files and connections for you, even when an exception happens. The resource must implement `AutoCloseable`. If both the body and `close` fail, the close error is attached to the first one as a suppressed exception.

example.title: A resource that is closed automatically, in reverse order

/java/core-java/exceptions/custom-except.def: A custom exception is your own exception class, named after the problem, such as `InsufficientFundsException`. It can carry extra data so the caller knows exactly what went wrong.

example.title: An exception that carries the missing amount

/java/core-java/exceptions/exception-cha.def: Exception chaining means wrapping a low-level exception inside a higher-level one and keeping the original as its cause. The caller gets a meaningful message, and the full story is still available through `getCause()`.

example.title: Wrapping a parse error in a service error

/java/core-java/exceptions/multi-catch.def: A multi-catch handles several exception types in one block, written `catch (A | B e)`. Use it when the handling is the same. You can also rethrow an exception after logging it, so callers still see the failure.

example.title: One handler for two kinds of failure

/java/core-java/immutability/immutable-c.def: An immutable class creates objects that never change. Make the class `final`, make all fields `private final`, set them in the constructor, and give no setters. Methods that "change" the object return a new one.

example.title: A Money class where plus() returns a new object

/java/core-java/immutability/defensive-c.def: A defensive copy means copying a mutable object when it goes into or comes out of your class. Without it, the caller keeps a reference to your internal data and can change it behind your back, even if the field is `final`.

example.title: Copying a list on the way in, and exposing a read-only view

/java/core-java/immutability/immutable-c.def: `List.of`, `Set.of` and `Map.of` create collections that cannot be changed. `List.copyOf` makes an independent immutable snapshot, while `Collections.unmodifiableList` is only a read-only window onto a list that can still change.

example.title: List.copyOf is a snapshot, unmodifiableList is a live view

/java/core-java/immutability/withers.def: A "wither" is a method that returns a copy of an immutable object with one value changed, for example `withEmail(...)`. It gives you the convenience of updating without making the object mutable.

example.title: Changing one field by creating a modified copy

/java/core-java/immutability/string-immu.def: A Java `String` can never be changed after it is created. Methods like `toUpperCase()` or `replace()` return a new String and leave the original alone. Use `StringBuilder` when you build text in a loop.

example.title: String methods return new strings; StringBuilder changes in place

/java/core-java/streams-and-lambdas/lamb.def: A lambda is a short piece of code you can pass around, written `(input) -> result`. It replaces a bulky anonymous class when an interface has just one method.

example.title: Sorting with a lambda instead of an anonymous class

/java/core-java/streams-and-lambdas/func.def: A functional interface has exactly one abstract method, so a lambda can stand in for it. Java provides common ones: `Function` (input to output), `Predicate` (yes or no), `Supplier` (gives a value) and `Consumer` (uses a value).

example.title: The four built-in shapes, and your own

/java/core-java/streams-and-lambdas/meth.def: A method reference is a shorter lambda that just calls an existing method, written `Class::method`. Use it when the lambda would only pass its argument straight to that method.

example.title: Replacing small lambdas with method references

/java/core-java/streams-and-lambdas/map-.def: A stream is a pipeline for data. `filter` keeps items that match, `map` changes each item, and `collect` or `toList` gathers the result. Nothing runs until that final step.

example.title: Names of adults, in capitals

/java/core-java/streams-and-lambdas/grou.def: Collectors turn a stream into a result. `groupingBy` splits items into groups, `counting` counts them, `joining` builds one string, and `toMap` builds a map.

example.title: Group words by length, count them, and join them

/java/core-java/streams-and-lambdas/flat.def: `flatMap` turns each item into a stream and joins all of those streams into one. Use it when each item holds a list and you want one flat list of everything.

example.title: From a list of orders to one list of items

/java/core-java/streams-and-lambdas/redu.def: `reduce` combines all items of a stream into a single value by applying an operation again and again, such as adding numbers. It needs a starting value and a rule for combining two values.

example.title: Adding numbers, and finding the longest word

/java/core-java/streams-and-lambdas/opti.def: `Optional` is a box that holds a value or is empty. It makes "there may be no result" visible in the method signature, so callers must decide what to do instead of hitting a `NullPointerException`.

example.title: Finding a user that may not exist

/java/core-java/streams-and-lambdas/para.def: A parallel stream splits the work across several CPU cores. It can speed up heavy calculations on large data, but it adds overhead, so it is slower for small lists. Never use it for blocking calls or with shared mutable state.

example.title: Same result, computed on several cores

/java/core-java/modern-java/var.def: `var` lets the compiler work out the type of a local variable from the value on the right, so you do not repeat a long type name. The variable is still strongly typed; it is just not written out.

example.title: Less typing, same safety

/java/core-java/modern-java/records.def: A record is a short way to declare a class that only carries data. You list the fields once, and Java creates the constructor, getters, `equals`, `hashCode` and `toString`. The fields are final.

example.title: A data class in one line

/java/core-java/modern-java/text-blocks.def: A text block is a multi-line string written between triple quotes. It keeps line breaks and removes the common indentation, so JSON, SQL and HTML are easy to read in code without `\n` and escaped quotes.

example.title: A JSON string without escaping

/java/core-java/modern-java/switch-expre.def: A switch expression returns a value and uses `->`, so there is no fall-through and no `break`. The compiler checks that every case is covered, which makes it safer than the old switch statement.

example.title: Turning a day into a number of hours

/java/core-java/modern-java/sealed-class.def: A sealed class or interface lists exactly which classes may extend it, using `permits`. The compiler then knows every possible subtype, so a `switch` over it is checked for completeness without a `default`.

example.title: A closed set of payment types

/java/core-java/modern-java/default-and-.def: Since Java 8 an interface can contain methods with a body. A `default` method gives implementing classes a ready-made behaviour they may override, and a `static` method belongs to the interface itself. This let Java add new methods to old interfaces without breaking existing classes.

example.title: An interface with a default method and a static helper

/java/core-java/modern-java/date-and-tim.def: The `java.time` package (Java 8) replaced the old `Date` and `Calendar`. Its classes, such as `LocalDate`, `LocalDateTime`, `Duration` and `Period`, are immutable and clear, and they handle months, days and formatting correctly.

example.title: Adding months, measuring days and formatting a date

/java/core-java/modern-java/collection-f.def: `List.of`, `Set.of` and `Map.of` (Java 9) create small immutable collections in one line. They do not allow `null`, and `Set.of` and `Map.of` reject duplicates.

example.title: Immutable collections in one line

/java/core-java/modern-java/private-inte.def: Since Java 9 an interface can have `private` methods. They let several default methods share code inside the interface without exposing that code to anyone else.

example.title: Two default methods sharing one private helper

/java/core-java/modern-java/stream-takew.def: `takeWhile` keeps items from the start of a stream until a condition first fails. `dropWhile` skips items from the start until the condition first fails and keeps the rest. Java 9 also added `Stream.iterate` with a stop condition.

example.title: Cutting a stream at the first item that fails a test

/java/core-java/modern-java/optional-add.def: Java 9 added `ifPresentOrElse` (do one thing if there is a value, another if not), `or` (try another Optional) and `stream` (turn an Optional into a stream of zero or one items).

example.title: Handling both cases without an if statement

/java/core-java/modern-java/try-with-res.def: Before Java 9 a resource had to be declared inside the `try (...)` parentheses. Now you can pass a variable that already exists, as long as it is final or effectively final, and Java still closes it for you.

example.title: Using an existing variable as the resource

/java/core-java/modern-java/modules.def: The Java Platform Module System (Java 9) groups packages into named modules. A `module-info.java` file says what the module needs (`requires`) and which packages other modules may use (`exports`), so internal packages stay hidden.

example.title: A module that exports one package and keeps another internal

/java/core-java/modern-java/copyof-and-u.def: Java 10 added `List.copyOf`, `Set.copyOf` and `Map.copyOf` to make an immutable copy of an existing collection. It also added `Collectors.toUnmodifiableList`, `toUnmodifiableSet` and `toUnmodifiableMap` for streams.

example.title: Copying a list and collecting a stream into an immutable list

/java/core-java/modern-java/string-metho.def: Java 11 added useful `String` methods: `isBlank` (empty or only spaces), `strip` (trim that understands Unicode), `lines` (split into lines as a stream) and `repeat`.

example.title: The four new String helpers

/java/core-java/modern-java/http-client.def: Java 11 made `java.net.http.HttpClient` a standard part of Java. It sends HTTP requests, supports HTTP/2, and can work synchronously or asynchronously, so you no longer need an extra library for simple calls.

example.title: Calling a small local server (so it runs without internet)

/java/core-java/modern-java/files-readst.def: Java 11 added `Files.readString` and `Files.writeString` to read or write a whole text file in one line, with UTF-8 by default.

example.title: Write a file and read it back

/java/core-java/modern-java/predicate-no.def: `Predicate.not` (Java 11) reverses a condition so you can use it with a method reference, for example `filter(Predicate.not(String::isBlank))` instead of writing a lambda with `!`.

example.title: Keeping only the non-blank lines

/java/core-java/modern-java/var-in-lambd.def: Java 11 lets you write `var` for lambda parameters. It does not change behaviour, but it lets you add annotations such as `@NonNull` to a parameter without writing out its type.

example.title: Using var for lambda parameters

/java/core-java/modern-java/single-file-.def: Java 11 can run a `.java` file directly with `java Hello.java`. It compiles the file in memory and runs it, which is handy for small scripts and for learning.

example.title: One file, one command

/java/core-java/modern-java/collectors-t.def: `Collectors.teeing` (Java 12) runs two collectors over the same stream at once and combines their two results. It saves you from going through the data twice.

example.title: Count and total in one pass, then compute the average

/java/core-java/modern-java/string-inden.def: Java 12 added `String.indent` (add or remove leading spaces on every line) and `String.transform` (pass a string through a function so you can chain steps).

example.title: Indenting text and chaining a transformation

/java/core-java/modern-java/helpful-npe-.def: Since Java 14 (on by default from Java 15) a `NullPointerException` tells you exactly which part was null, for example "because the return value of Demo.findCity() is null". You no longer have to guess in a long chain of calls.

example.title: The exception now names the null part

/java/core-java/modern-java/pattern-matc.def: Pattern matching for `instanceof` (Java 16) checks a type and gives you a typed variable in one step. You no longer need a separate cast after the check.

example.title: No cast after instanceof

/java/core-java/modern-java/stream-tolis.def: `Stream.toList()` (Java 16) ends a stream with an unmodifiable list, so you no longer write `collect(Collectors.toList())` for the common case.

example.title: A shorter way to finish a stream

/java/core-java/modern-java/random-gener.def: Java 17 added the `RandomGenerator` interface and a factory with many modern algorithms. You pick an algorithm by name and can seed it, so the same seed always gives the same numbers.

example.title: A seeded generator gives repeatable numbers

/java/core-java/modern-java/utf8-by-defa.def: Since Java 18 the default character set of the JVM is UTF-8 on every operating system. Before, it depended on the machine (for example Windows-1252), so the same code could read text differently on different computers.

example.title: The default charset is now always UTF-8

/java/core-java/modern-java/virtual-thre.def: Virtual threads (Java 21) are very cheap threads managed by the JVM. When one waits, for example on a network call, it steps aside so another can run. You can run tens of thousands at once with simple blocking code.

example.title: 10,000 tasks that each wait, run at the same time

/java/core-java/modern-java/pattern-matc.def: Pattern matching for `switch` (Java 21) lets a `switch` choose code by the type of a value, and even add a condition with `when`. It also handles `null` as a case.

example.title: A switch that picks code by type and condition

/java/core-java/modern-java/record-patte.def: A record pattern (Java 21) takes a record apart inside `instanceof` or `switch`, giving you its fields as variables. Patterns can be nested, so you can unpack a record that holds other records in one step.

example.title: Unpacking a Line made of two Points

/java/core-java/modern-java/sequenced-co.def: Sequenced collections (Java 21) add a common way to work with the first and last element and to reverse any collection that has a defined order. New methods include `getFirst`, `getLast`, `addFirst`, `addLast` and `reversed`.

example.title: First, last and reversed on a list and a LinkedHashMap

/java/core-java/modern-java/unnamed-vari.def: An underscore `_` (Java 22) marks a variable you must declare but will never use, such as a loop variable, a caught exception or a part of a pattern. It tells the reader, and the compiler, that the value is ignored on purpose.

example.title: Underscore for values you do not need

/java/core-java/modern-java/markdown-doc.def: Since Java 23 you can write documentation comments in Markdown by starting each line with `///` instead of the old `/** ... */` with HTML. Lists, bold, links and code blocks use normal Markdown.

example.title: A documentation comment written in Markdown

/java/core-java/modern-java/stream-gathe.def: A gatherer (Java 24) is a custom step in a stream pipeline that can group, window or carry state between items, which the old `map` and `filter` could not do. `Gatherers` ships ready-made ones such as `windowFixed` and `windowSliding`.

example.title: Grouping items into windows

/java/core-java/modern-java/scoped-value.def: A scoped value (Java 25) shares data with the code you call, for example the current user, without passing it as a parameter. The value is fixed for the duration of one `run` and is safe to share with virtual threads, which makes it a cleaner replacement for `ThreadLocal`.

example.title: The current user, available to every method inside run()

/java/core-java/modern-java/flexible-con.def: Flexible constructor bodies (Java 25) let you run statements before calling `super(...)` or `this(...)`, as long as they do not use the object being built. You can validate or compute arguments first instead of using awkward static helper methods.

example.title: Validating an argument before calling super

/java/core-java/modern-java/module-impor.def: A module import (Java 25) imports every public class that a module exports with one line, `import module java.base;`. It saves long lists of imports in small programs and scripts.

example.title: One import line instead of five

/java/core-java/modern-java/compact-sour.def: Compact source files (Java 25) let a small program be just a `void main()` method, with no class declaration and no `public static`. It removes the ceremony from a first program or a script.

example.title: A whole program with no class around it
